binary-tree.introduction: A Binary Tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.
binary-tree.intuition: Think of a corporate hierarchy or a family tree where each person can have at most two direct subordinates or children.

walkthrough.description: The topmost node of the tree.
Each node can have 0, 1, or 2 children.
Nodes with no children are called leaf nodes.

dryRun.input: Node A with left B and right C

complexities.analysis: Accessing elements takes time proportional to the depth of the tree. Worst case (a skewed tree) takes O(N).

mistakes: Not checking for null pointers before accessing a node's left or right children.
edgeCases: Tree with only a root node
tips: Almost all binary tree problems can be solved using recursion. Think about the base case (node == null).

bst.introduction: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where every node in the left subtree is smaller than the root, and every node in the right subtree is larger.
bst.intuition: It works like searching in a dictionary or a phone book. If you are looking for 'M' and you are at 'K', you only need to search the right half.

walkthrough.description: Compare the target value with the current node's value.
If target < node.val, go left. If target > node.val, go right.
If target == node.val, return the node.

steps: Root is 5. 3 < 5, so go left to 2.
Current is 2. 3 > 2, so go right to 3.

complexities.analysis: Average search, insertion, and deletion takes O(log N) due to halving the search space. In the worst case (unbalanced tree), it degenerates to O(N).

mistakes: Assuming an inorder traversal of any binary tree is sorted (it's only sorted for BSTs).
edgeCases: Searching for a value not in the BST
tips: An inorder traversal of a BST yields a sorted array. This is a very common trick for BST problems.

avl-tree.introduction: An AVL tree is a self-balancing Binary Search Tree where the difference between heights of left and right subtrees cannot be more than one for all nodes.
avl-tree.intuition: If a tree gets too lopsided, operations become slow (O(N)). AVL trees automatically perform rotations to pull the tree back into a balanced shape.

walkthrough.description: Insert the node like a standard BST.
Update the height of the current node.
Calculate the balance factor (left_height - right_height). If it's > 1 or < -1, perform rotations to rebalance.

steps: Insert 2 (left of 3). Balance factor of 3 is 1.
Insert 1 (left of 2). Balance factor of 3 is 2. (Left-Left Case)
Right rotate around 3. 2 becomes root, 1 is left, 3 is right.

complexities.analysis: Because the tree is strictly balanced, all operations (search, insert, delete) take O(log N) time.

tree-traversal.introduction: Tree traversal involves visiting every node in a tree exactly once. The common depth-first methods are Pre-order, In-order, and Post-order.
tree-traversal.intuition: Think of exploring a maze. Do you want to process the room you are in first (Pre), explore the left path, process the room, then the right (In), or explore all paths fully before processing the room (Post)?

walkthrough.description: Left, Root, Right. For a BST, this visits nodes in ascending order.
Root, Left, Right. Useful for copying a tree.
Left, Right, Root. Useful for deleting a tree, as you delete children before the parent.

steps: Go right from 2 to 3. 3 has no left. Print 3.

complexities.analysis: O(N) time to visit all nodes. O(H) space for the recursion stack, where H is the height of the tree.

code.python:
def inorder(root):
    if not root: return
    inorder(root.left)
    print(root.val, end=" ")
    inorder(root.right)

mistakes: Confusing the order of the recursive calls for the different traversals.
tips: If asked to do this iteratively instead of recursively, you will need to use an explicit Stack.

lca.introduction: The Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes p and q in a tree is the lowest node that has both p and q as descendants.
lca.intuition: If two people want to find their closest shared relative, they look up their family trees until their paths intersect.

walkthrough.description: If root is null, p, or q, return root.
Recursively search the left and right subtrees for p and q.
If both left and right return a node, the current root is the LCA. If only one returns a node, pass that node up.

dryRun.input: LCA of 5 and 1 in Tree where 3 is root, 5 is left, 1 is right
steps: Root is 3. Search left for 5 and 1. Search right for 5 and 1.
Since both sides returned non-null, 3 is the LCA.

complexities.analysis: We may have to visit every node in the tree to find p and q.

code.python:
def lowestCommonAncestor(root, p, q):
    if not root or root == p or root == q: return root
    left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
    right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)
    if left and right: return root
    return left or right

mistakes: Assuming p and q are guaranteed to be in the tree (if not, this algorithm might return a false positive).
edgeCases: p is a descendant of q (or vice versa)
tips: For a BST, this is even easier (O(log N)): just find the first node whose value is strictly between p.val and q.val.

tree-diameter.introduction: The diameter of a tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in a tree. This path may or may not pass through the root.
tree-diameter.intuition: The longest path passing through any given node is the max depth of its left subtree plus the max depth of its right subtree. We calculate this for every node and keep track of the maximum.

walkthrough.description: Write a recursive function that returns the height of a subtree.
Inside the function, update a global (or passed by reference) variable with left_height + right_height.
Return max(left_height, right_height) + 1 to the parent call.

steps: Depth of 4 and 5 is 1. Diameter at 2 is 1+1 = 2.
Depth of 2 is 2. Depth of 3 is 1.

complexities.analysis: O(N) because we visit each node exactly once using a bottom-up approach.

code.python:
def diameterOfBinaryTree(root):
    max_diam = 0
    def depth(node):
        nonlocal max_diam
        if not node: return 0
        left = depth(node.left)
        right = depth(node.right)
        max_diam = max(max_diam, left + right)
        return max(left, right) + 1
    depth(root)
    return max_diam

mistakes: Assuming the diameter must pass through the root node (it doesn't have to).
tips: This pattern (returning height while simultaneously updating a global max variable) is incredibly common in tree problems.

balanced-tree.introduction: A height-balanced binary tree is a binary tree in which the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by no more than 1.
balanced-tree.intuition: Similar to finding the diameter, we recursively find the height of the left and right subtrees. If at any point the difference is > 1, the tree is unbalanced.

walkthrough.description: Write a function that returns the height of a tree.
If a subtree is unbalanced, return -1 (a sentinel value).
If a parent receives -1 from any child, it immediately returns -1.

steps: At 2: Left depth 1, right depth 0. Diff 1. Balanced. Depth 2.
At 1: Left depth 2, right depth 0. Diff 2. Unbalanced! Return -1.

complexities.analysis: O(N) time because we do a single bottom-up traversal. If we did top-down, it would be O(N^2).

code.python:
def isBalanced(root):
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return 0
        left = dfs(node.left)
        if left == -1: return -1
        right = dfs(node.right)
        if right == -1: return -1
        if abs(left - right) > 1: return -1
        return max(left, right) + 1
    return dfs(root) != -1

mistakes: Using a top-down O(N^2) approach by calculating height repeatedly for every node.
tips: Always mention that your bottom-up approach is O(N) because it reuses height calculations, demonstrating optimization skills.

tree-views.introduction: Tree views (Top, Bottom, Left, Right) involve looking at a 3D representation of a tree from a specific angle and returning the nodes visible from that angle.
tree-views.intuition: Left/Right views are easily solved with Level Order Traversal (BFS) by taking the first/last node of each level. Top/Bottom views use BFS but keep track of the horizontal distance (x-coordinate) of each node.

walkthrough.description: Do a BFS. Add the last node of each level queue to the result.
Do a BFS while tracking horizontal distance (HD). Store the first node seen at each HD in a map.

complexities.analysis: BFS processes each node once. The queue and result arrays take O(N) space.

mistakes: Using DFS for Top/Bottom views without tracking depth properly, causing nodes lower in the tree to overwrite higher nodes.
edgeCases: Nodes overlapping at the same horizontal distance in Top/Bottom view.
tips: Right side view can also be done via DFS by strictly exploring Right before Left and tracking max depth seen so far.

serialize-tree.introduction: Serialization is the process of converting a data structure into a sequence of bits or a string so that it can be stored or transmitted and later reconstructed.
serialize-tree.intuition: We can use a Pre-order traversal to visit every node. To reconstruct the exact shape of the tree, we must also record null pointers (e.g., using 'N' or 'null').

walkthrough.description: Visit root, then left, then right.
If a node is null, append a special character like 'N' to the string.
Join all values with a delimiter like a comma.

steps: Right of 1 is 3... and so on.

complexities.analysis: O(N) to traverse and build the string.

mistakes: Not using a delimiter (like comma), making it impossible to distinguish between the value '12' and the values '1', '2'.
tips: BFS (Level Order) serialization is also very common and is exactly how LeetCode formats its tree test cases in arrays.

deserialize-tree.introduction: Deserialization is the reverse of serialization: reconstructing the binary tree from its string representation.
deserialize-tree.intuition: If we serialized using Pre-order (Root, Left, Right), we can rebuild it exactly the same way. We consume the string array left to right, building the root first, then its left child, then its right child.

walkthrough.description: Split the serialized string by the delimiter (comma) into an array or queue.
Pop the front value. If it's 'N', return null. Otherwise, create a node.
Recursively call build for node.left and node.right.

complexities.analysis: O(N) to parse the string and create N nodes.
